title: Gulf Ceasefire Unravels as Iran Fires Missiles at Kuwait and Bahrain. India’s Seafarers Pay the Price.
excerpt: Three Indian sailors are dead, 20,000 seafarers remain stranded in the Persian Gulf, and the fragile US-Iran deal is falling apart — leaving New Delhi caught between its closest strategic partner and its citizens’ safety.
body:
The fragile US-Iran ceasefire signed barely two weeks ago is coming apart at the seams. On Sunday, Iran launched ballistic missiles at American military bases in Kuwait and Bahrain, capping three days of renewed fighting that began when Tehran attacked a cargo ship on a UN-designated safe route through the Strait of Hormuz. An apartment building in Muharraq, Bahrain, was reduced to rubble. While both sides have agreed — again — to stop shooting, the damage to the peace process may already be done. And for thousands of Indian seafarers stranded in the Persian Gulf, the promised rescue has stalled, leaving many families in India anxious about their loved ones' safety and financial stability.

## A Ceasefire Built on Sand

The June 17 memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran was supposed to be a turning point. The 14-point framework gave both sides 60 days to extend an earlier ceasefire, discuss Iran’s nuclear program, and negotiate a permanent settlement. Crucially, it committed both parties to reopening the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway that once carried a fifth of the world’s oil — without tolls. This was particularly vital for global trade, including India's significant energy imports.

The accord was immediately tested. Iran established a “Persian Gulf Strait Authority” to manage ship transit and insisted that all vessels inform Tehran before crossing. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned that safe passage would only be guaranteed on routes it had declared. Washington, backed by the UN’s International Maritime Organization (IMO), pushed an alternative corridor along the Omani coast — setting up a direct clash over who controls the waterway. This dispute directly impacts the safety and operational routes for thousands of Indian seafarers who regularly navigate these waters.

## Three Days of Escalation

The latest violence erupted on Thursday when Iran struck the Singapore-flagged cargo ship Ever Lovely with a drone as it navigated the UN-backed route near Oman. The IMO, which had begun evacuating hundreds of stranded ships and thousands of seafarers, immediately paused operations. “The safety of the seafarers remains paramount,” IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez said, a sentiment echoed by many Indian families desperate for news.

The United States responded with airstrikes on Friday, targeting Iranian radar sites, missile positions, and drone storage facilities along the strait. Iran escalated on Saturday with drone attacks on Bahrain, and then on Sunday launched ballistic missiles at the Ali al-Salem Air Base in Kuwait and the headquarters of the US Fifth Fleet in Bahrain.

Kuwait intercepted two incoming missiles. In Bahrain, a top-floor apartment in Muharraq was destroyed, though officials reported no casualties. Iran warned it could bring peace talks to a “complete halt.”

By Sunday evening, both sides had agreed to stand down — for now. “We decided to stop all the kinetic activity,” a senior US official told Axios. But whether the agreement holds remains deeply uncertain, leaving the fate of stranded Indian seafarers hanging in the balance.

## Doha Talks in Doubt

On Monday, President Trump dispatched his son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff to lead a negotiating team to Doha. Iran confirmed it was sending a technical delegation to Qatar — but said the visit had “no relation” to the Americans’ presence and that “no negotiation meetings at any level” were scheduled with the US side. Trump himself offered a characteristically hedged assessment: “The meeting in Doha is going to be perhaps important, perhaps not.”

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, meanwhile, declared that $6 billion of $12 billion in frozen Iranian assets held in Qatar would be released — calling the memorandum “a great victory for the Iranian people.” Oil prices rose more than 1 percent after the weekend hostilities, underscoring the global market’s fragile confidence in the accord. This volatility directly impacts the global economy, including the cost of living for NRIs and the remittances they send home.

## India Caught Between Partner and Citizens

For India, the escalation compounds an already acute crisis. Even before the ceasefire was signed, three Indian seafarers had died in a US attack on the vessel MT Settebello, prompting New Delhi to lodge a formal protest and summon US Chargé d’Affaires Jason Meeks. “The welfare of our seafaring community is very important, and the attacks that are happening must stop,” MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said. The human cost of this conflict is deeply felt by Indian families, many of whom rely on the income of their loved ones working on these ships.

The numbers are stark. According to the IMO, at least 14 seafarers have been killed and over 40 commercial vessels attacked since the conflict began in February. Insurance giant Allianz estimates that some 1,150 cargo vessels and 20,000 seafarers remain stranded in the Persian Gulf, with trapped ships and cargo valued at roughly $125 billion.

India has the world’s largest seafarer workforce, with tens of thousands of its citizens working on commercial vessels that regularly transit the Strait of Hormuz. Beyond the maritime workforce, an estimated 9 million Indians live and work in the Gulf states — the largest diaspora concentration in the world. Any widening of the conflict directly threatens their safety and livelihoods, impacting remittances and family ties back home. "My brother is stuck there, and we haven't heard from him in days," shared a worried relative of an Indian seafarer from Kerala, highlighting the profound personal toll. "We just want him to come home safe."

The economic stakes are equally severe. India imports roughly 60 percent of its crude oil from the Middle East, and the Hormuz crisis has already pushed global oil prices above $100 a barrel. Higher energy costs feed directly into domestic inflation, freight charges, and the cost of everyday goods — hitting Indian consumers and businesses from the pump to the kitchen table. This also affects the purchasing power of remittances sent by NRIs, as their families in India face rising costs.

## What Comes Next

The Doha talks — if they happen — represent the best remaining chance to salvage the ceasefire. But the gap between Washington and Tehran is widening. Iran insists it alone must govern passage through the Strait of Hormuz. The United States says any final deal must guarantee free navigation. France has offered to help de-mine the strait, drawing an immediate rebuke from Tehran, which says that responsibility belongs exclusively to Iran under the 14-point plan.

For India, the crisis demands a difficult diplomatic balancing act. The United States remains one of New Delhi’s most important strategic partners, particularly in defence, technology, and Indo-Pacific security. But when American military operations endanger Indian citizens on commercial vessels, that partnership is tested in ways that no amount of strategic rhetoric can smooth over. India’s call for “dialogue and diplomacy” and “unimpeded access through the Strait of Hormuz in keeping with international law” is clear enough. Whether anyone is listening, and how quickly a resolution can be found to ensure the safety of its citizens, is another matter.
